summary: Some systems, such as WebRTC, receive several kinds of packets on a single port and must tell them apart. RFC 7983 defined a scheme for separating DTLS, STUN, SRTP, ZRTP and TURN traffic. This document updates RFC 7983 and RFC 5764 so QUIC packets can share the same socket as well.

eli5.summary: Think of one mailbox that gets letters in several languages. This document teaches the mail sorter how to spot one more language, QUIC, so it goes to the right reader.

questions: can quic share a port with dtls and stun
how to demultiplex quic and rtp packets
subtitle: Teaches the receiver's first-byte sorting rule to recognize QUIC packets arriving on the same port as STUN, DTLS and RTP.

tldr.problem: RFC 7983 let a receiver tell DTLS, STUN, SRTP, ZRTP and TURN channel packets apart on one port, but it had no place for QUIC.
tldr.mechanism: The first byte of each packet picks the protocol. QUIC gets the ranges 80 to 127 and 192 to 255, and 64 to 79 is QUIC unless the packet comes from a TURN server.
tldr.outcome: QUIC can share a socket with the other protocols, provided endpoints do not send the grease_quic_bit transport parameter.

today: RFC 9443 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 7983 and RFC 5764.

sections.title: Sharing One Port with QUIC
sections.content:
RFC 7983 defines how a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) receiver can demultiplex DTLS, STUN, SRTP/SRTCP, ZRTP and TURN channel packets on a single port. This document updates RFC 7983 and RFC 5764 so that QUIC can use the same port.

One use case is WebRTC, where SRTP carries audio and video while peer-to-peer QUIC exchanges data. SRTP is keyed with DTLS-SRTP, so SRTP/SRTCP, STUN, TURN, DTLS and QUIC all share a port. Another is QUIC used for data as well as RTP/RTCP, where STUN, TURN and QUIC share the port.
sections.eli5: Several kinds of messages arrive at one door. The doorman needs a rule to know which room each one belongs in, and now QUIC needs a room too.

sections.title: The First-Byte Sorting Rule
sections.content:
The receiver looks at the first byte of each packet. Values 0 to 3 are STUN, 16 to 19 are ZRTP, 20 to 63 are DTLS, and 128 to 191 are RTP (or RTCP, if both are multiplexed on the port). New in this document, values 80 to 127 and 192 to 255 are QUIC. Values 4 to 15 are dropped. Anything that matches no known range MUST be dropped, and an alert MAY be logged.

The range 64 to 79 is special: it is a TURN channel packet if it comes from the source IP address and port of a responding TURN server, and QUIC otherwise.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a number. The sorter reads that number and sends the message to the matching reader.

sections.title: What Changed in RFC 7983
sections.content:
Section 3 of this document replaces the demultiplexing text in Section 7 of RFC 7983 (which in turn updates RFC 5764) using an OLD TEXT and NEW TEXT format. The old text sent 64 to 79 to TURN Channel only, and had no QUIC range. The new text adds QUIC at 80 to 127 and 192 to 255, makes 64 to 79 depend on the source address, and adds an explicit drop range for 4 to 15.

It also adds a note to Figure 3: endpoints that wish to demultiplex QUIC MUST NOT send the grease_quic_bit transport parameter described in RFC 9287.
sections.eli5: The sorter's rule book got a new page. It now has a place for QUIC and a rule for the shared number range.

sections.title: TURN Channels and QUIC Greasing
sections.content:
TURN channels use a 4-byte prefix instead of the standard 36-byte STUN overhead. RFC 7983 gave them first-byte values 64 to 79. Without QUIC bit greasing, the first byte of a QUIC packet (for example a short header packet in QUIC v1 or v2) can be anywhere from 64 to 127, so it overlaps that range.

The RFC says this overlap is not a problem in practice. TURN channel packets only come from a TURN server to which allocation and channel-binding requests were sent, so a client only needs to separate STUN from TURN channel packets for that source address and port. Other protocols, QUIC included, will not be sent from it.

The scheme is compatible with QUIC version 2 but not with QUIC bit greasing. Endpoints that want to multiplex on their socket MUST NOT send the grease_quic_bit transport parameter.
sections.eli5: Two kinds of mail could look alike, but one kind only ever arrives from one known sender. So the sorter checks who sent it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The added logic could introduce issues beyond those in RFC 7983. If misimplemented, it could misclassify packets and expose protocol handlers to unexpected input.

When QUIC is used only for data, the TLS exchange inside QUIC derives keys that protect only QUIC data packets, so it should not affect SRTP or DTLS-SRTP key derivation if properly implemented. If a future specification used it to derive SRTP keys, a flaw in the QUIC implementation could harm both transport and SRTP key derivation.

For IANA, references to RFC 7983 in the "TLS ContentType" registry were replaced with this document.
sections.eli5: If the sorter makes a mistake, a reader might get a message it cannot handle, so it has to be built carefully.
